claims.text: A machine-learning model incorporating oxygen content and defect-density parameters will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately than conventional analytical models.
Conventional analytical models for HfNbTaTiZr assume ideal, defect-free crystals.
Electrical transport from 0 to 200 K is dominated by quantum scattering.
Electrical transport from 300 to 1200 K is dominated by thermal phonon and defect scattering.
The proposed model will use temperature, alloy composition, oxygen level, and estimated defect density as input features.
The model is intended to cover bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen.
Features representing intrinsic thermal vibrations and extrinsic defects or oxygen impurities can capture their respective scattering effects.
The feature representation can capture the interplay between low-temperature quantum scattering and high-temperature defect-assisted transport.
Existing conductivity datasets cover both specified temperature regimes.
Training on conductivity data while including defect-related features will allow the model to resolve quantum, phonon, and defect-scattering contributions.
Representing defect and impurity effects produces a more realistic description of conduction than a perfect-lattice model.
The model will reduce disagreement with experimental conductivity measurements in both temperature regimes.
The model will improve prediction of conductivity behavior from 0 to 200 K.
The model will retain an accuracy advantage from 300 to 1200 K by representing variable defect scattering.
Conventional analytical models include only phonon scattering at high temperatures.
The model may require modification for impurity concentrations or defect densities substantially outside its training distribution.
Poor characterization of defect density or oxygen distribution may limit conductivity-prediction accuracy.
A held-out HfNbTaTiZr sample containing 1 wt.% oxygen will be benchmarked at 150 K and 900 K.
Exceeding an uncertainty margin or predefined percentage-error threshold at either benchmark temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
